clue.text: Pares back, stingy – 'until tomorrow'?

indicators.note: going back means travelling the opposite way, so the letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: to pare fruit is to peel it, so pares = peels
a tight person is mean with money

explanation.surface: A miser trims spending and puts everything off until tomorrow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pare back' reads as one phrase meaning cut down, but 'back' is the reversal signal working on the synonym for 'Pares'. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying goodnight with this phrase is a farewell meant to last only until the next morning, when you meet again.

clue.text: Tournament player to give up, did you say?

indicators.note: asking whether something was said points to how a word sounds rather than how it is written

blocks.note: to cede is to give up or surrender

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a tennis player in a tournament has just conceded the match.
explanation.walkthrough: CEDE and SEED are pronounced the same, though spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis and similar events, top-ranked entrants are placed in the draw so they avoid each other early; such a ranked competitor is called this.

clue.text: A border or two in the East End?

blocks.clueFragment: A border or two in the East End?
blocks.note: surface reading: some frontiers or margins found in east London
setter's reading: Cockneys drop an initial H, so a garden boundary of shrubs loses its first letter and sounds like a second word for border

explanation.walkthrough: The East End is the traditional working-class area of London, whose Cockney accent drops initial H; without its H a hedge becomes this word, which already means a border.
explanation.definitionFit: The outer limit or rim of a surface is its margin, which is a plain synonym for border.

clue.text: Round up chaps being tipsy and cocksure

indicators.note: a tipsy person staggers about, so the letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Herd together the lads who are drunk and full of swagger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round up' reads as an instruction to gather the chaps, but it is simply letters to be rearranged along with 'chaps'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone extremely pleased with themselves, which matches the brash self-confidence of being cocksure.

clue.text: 'Alternatively stained' (messy)

indicators.note: something messy is disordered, so the letters are jumbled out of their given order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: It reads like a dictionary or style note offering 'stained' as an alternative word, with a messy label.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like a phrase being glossed, but 'Alternatively' is the definition and the bracketed word is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean as a substitute or in place of something else, offering another option.

clue.text: Executioner's game

blocks.note: first meaning: the official who carries out death by the noose
second meaning: the word-guessing pastime where wrong guesses build a gallows drawing

explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s looks possessive, as if the executioner owns a game, but it stands for 'is', linking two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the person who carries out hangings and a pencil-and-paper guessing pastime.

clue.text: In France, quietly left duck: it's a disaster

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one pair goes inside the other

blocks.note: F is the international vehicle code for France
p (piano) is the musical marking for quietly
L is the standard abbreviation for left
a duck in cricket is a score of zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: Someone in France slips away quietly and ducks out, and it turns into a fiasco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In France' looks like scene-setting but is a container instruction: F and P enclose L and O. A duck is a batsman's score of nought in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: A total failure, such as a play or film that bombs, is commonly called by this informal noun.

clue.text: Publicans procure facilities

blocks.note: to land a job or deal is to procure it
the facilities is a euphemism for toilets, and the ladies is a women's toilet

explanation.surface: Pub owners arranging the provision of amenities for their customers.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'the Ladies' is the women's toilet, which a polite speaker calls 'the facilities'.
explanation.definitionFit: Women who run a pub or inn are traditionally called by this title, so they are female publicans.

clue.text: Demonstrates musical skill; barely pays out

indicators.note: something put out of place is disturbed, so these letters leave their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A musician who shows real talent but whose gigs scarcely earn anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pays out' reads as a phrasal verb about spending, but 'out' instructs a rearrangement of 'barely pays'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who performs a tune without written music, purely from memory and listening, shows considerable natural musical talent.

clue.text: Fascinating song singer composed

indicators.note: to compose is to put together or arrange, so the letters are arranged afresh

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A captivating tune that the performer wrote herself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composed' fits the musical surface as songwriting, which hides its role as the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something absorbing holds all your attention, which is a close synonym for captivating or gripping.

clue.text: Perhaps Pavlova going up and down?

indicators.note: a word that runs the same in both directions reads identically either way it travels

blocks.note: the name read in either direction comes out the same, so the description of a dancer rising and falling doubles as the letters' behaviour

explanation.surface: A ballerina bobbing up and down as she dances, or a meringue dessert rising and falling.
explanation.walkthrough: The name reads the same backwards as forwards. 'Going up and down' suits a dancer's leaps, and in a down clue it would mean reading upward or downward.
explanation.definitionFit: The celebrated Russian prima ballerina Pavlova had this first name, so it is one example of a person called Pavlova.

clue.text: Purposeful meal on foundation – but there's no answer

indicators.note: having none of something means it is missing, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a machine that is on is running or functioning
the foundation of a company is its founding or start-up
A is the abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: A business meal with a firm agenda, where nobody gets a straight reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Purposeful meal' looks like it might split, but it is the whole definition; 'on' alone is the first piece, and A drops out of the second.
explanation.definitionFit: A midday meal held so colleagues can discuss business while eating is a meal with a practical purpose.

clue.text: Finally scrawled argument on paper describing liberal fantasies

indicators.note: finally means at the very end, so only the closing letter is kept
placing one thing on another here sets the pieces side by side
to describe a circle is to draw round it, so one piece goes around another

blocks.note: the final letter of the word
a ream is a standard quantity of paper
to have words with someone is to argue
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A hasty scribbled polemic on the page about a liberal politician's utopian dreams.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Describing' in the geometric sense of drawing around: WORDS goes round L. In an across clue, 'argument on paper' puts the argument after the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Imaginary realms that exist only in the mind are illusions or daydreams, which is what fantasies are.

clue.text: Monet painting might provide this depiction of Elvis?

blocks.note: first meaning: the fleeting visual sense a Monet canvas aims to convey, the idea that named his movement
second meaning: an imitation of a celebrity such as Elvis by a comic or tribute act

explanation.walkthrough: Monet's 'Impression, Sunrise' named the Impressionist movement, and an impersonator does an Elvis turn of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the effect or idea a work leaves on a viewer and a mimic's comic imitation of a famous person.

clue.text: A Winter Olympic athlete eating muesli regularly? Not right now

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken
something eaten ends up inside the eater, so one piece is held within another

blocks.note: taken as written
figure skating and speed skating are Winter Olympic sports
the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: An Olympic ice skater munching breakfast cereal brushes off a question until later.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of muesli go inside the athlete just after SK.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a polite way to postpone a request, meaning the speaker will deal with it some other time.

clue.text: 'Everyman's regressive, small, far from fresh' ... and hurt!

indicators.note: regressing means going backwards, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: the setter, Everyman, speaking of himself: Everyman is = I am = I'M
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
something used is second-hand, not new

explanation.surface: The setter reads a review calling him backward, petty and stale, and feels wounded.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming himself means I or ME, so 'Everyman's' is 'I'm'; 'regressive' turns that round, not the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has been treated badly or abused has been wronged, which is a sense of hurt as a past participle.

clue.text: Led Yank about wanting wardrobe?

indicators.note: turned about means spun around, so the letters are moved into a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American is shown around while looking for a cupboard to hang clothes in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' here means lacking, not desiring: being without any wardrobe, in the sense of clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To do something without clothing is to lack a wardrobe, read as one's whole set of garments, so the adverb fits.

clue.text: A little conundrum, our scandalous tittle-tattle

indicators.note: a little of something is only a part of it, so the letters lie inside a longer run

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A small puzzle about our own juicy gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: The run is found across 'conundRUM OUR Scandalous', ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: Idle gossip and unverified stories passed from person to person are what tittle-tattle consists of.

clue.text: Father Christmas following echo somewhere in New Mexico

blocks.note: Father Christmas is the British name for Santa Claus
f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Santa Claus trailing after an echo in the American desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' looks like a placement instruction, but it supplies the abbreviation F used in references like 'p. 10 f.'.
explanation.definitionFit: The state capital of New Mexico bears this name, so it is a place located in that state.

clue.text: Major African nationalist, democratically elected liberating administrator, primarily?

definitions.text: Major African nationalist, democratically elected liberating administrator, primarily?

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter of each word is taken

blocks.clueFragment: Major African nationalist, democratically elected liberating administrator
blocks.note: the initial letters of the seven words

explanation.surface: A biography summary of a great African leader who won a free election and freed his people.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the instruction and the description: its initials spell the name, and it also describes the man.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson Mandela led the anti-apartheid struggle and became South Africa's first president chosen in a fully democratic vote.

clue.text: Irregularly stains, figuratively, one's senses

blocks.note: first meaning: as a verb, to streak or mottle with irregular colours like veined stone
second meaning: slang for sanity, which a person can 'lose'

explanation.walkthrough: 'Irregularly' and 'stains' together look like an anagram setup, but no rearrangement fits; it is a straight meaning of the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb describes mottling paper or meat with veined streaks, and the plural noun is slang for sanity or wits.

clue.text: Patience: second magical creature's getting key

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
an elf is a magical being from folklore
Control (Ctrl) is a key on a computer keyboard

explanation.surface: A fairy creature waits patiently, about to be handed a key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patience' could be the card game, but here it is the virtue.
explanation.definitionFit: Patience means restraining one's impulses and staying calm, which is the discipline of mastering one's own reactions.

clue.text: Told of destiny in outdoor event

indicators.note: something told is spoken, so the word comes by ear, not by spelling

blocks.note: fate is destiny

explanation.surface: A fortune teller at a summer fair tells people about their destiny.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage this word is pronounced like FATE. A fete is a village fair or garden party, often held to raise money.
explanation.definitionFit: A summer fair with stalls and games, usually held outdoors on a lawn or village green, is this kind of event.

clue.text: Divine figure sent up agreeable Spanish expression

indicators.note: in a down entry, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: si si is Spanish for yes yes, an agreeing response

explanation.surface: Someone mocks a god while murmuring a friendly Spanish phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' suggests mockery, but in a down clue it means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Isis was a major goddess of ancient Egyptian religion, worshipped as a mother and protector deity.

clue.text: Riot Act detains this Greek character

indicators.note: to detain is to hold inside, so the letters are held within the words

blocks.note: the run straddles the break between the two words

explanation.surface: Reading someone the Riot Act and locking up a particular Greek person.
explanation.walkthrough: The Riot Act was an old British law read aloud to disperse crowds; the letters sit across 'rIOT Act'.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth letter of the Greek alphabet, the equivalent of i, is a character of that alphabet.

clue.text: Europeans darn lapels in need of repair

indicators.note: something needing repair is broken, so these letters are in a damaged order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Europeans mending the worn lapels of their jackets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Darn' fits the sewing picture as mending, which hides that it is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: People from Lapland, the far northern region spanning Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, are inhabitants of the continent.

clue.text: Standard displayed at beginning/end of National Anthem?

indicators.note: a beginning is where something starts, so only its opening letter is used
the end is the final point, so only the closing letter is used

blocks.note: the first letter
the slash is read aloud as 'or', as in 'and/or'
the last letter

explanation.surface: A flag flown at the start or the close of the national anthem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standard' looks like a flag in this ceremonial picture, but it means a usual level. The slash is a piece of wordplay in its own right.
explanation.definitionFit: A usual or expected level of behaviour or quality is a benchmark, which is what a standard is.

clue.text: Awfully tense shrews run out for bulletins

indicators.note: out means gone away, so a letter is removed from the set
awfully suggests something done badly, so the letters end up badly ordered

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Highly-strung, nagging people dash outside to grab the latest news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run out' looks like a cricket dismissal or a dash, but R is removed from 'tense shrews' before the rest is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Printed single pages of news handed out to the public serve as brief reports or announcements, like bulletins.
